finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the dba role check is never enforced. Any caller who reaches /admin/drop can run DROP TABLE. The table name is also concatenated into the SQL string unsanitized, which allows SQL injection (for example a value like `x; DROP TABLE y`). The sibling handler vacuum checks the error and returns 403, so this handler is the one missing the check.
finding.source: HTTP request to /admin/drop with form value `t`, from any user (the user is only read from the context). The `t` value is attacker-controlled.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27. runSQL is a stub in this file, but it is the SQL execution point.

trace.note: Route /admin/drop is registered with http.HandleFunc and no auth middleware.
userFrom(r) reads the user from the request context.
Authorize(u, "dba") returns an error, but the return value is discarded, so execution continues.
The attacker-controlled `t` is concatenated into the DROP TABLE statement and passed to runSQL.

finding.guards_checked: Authorize is called but its result is unused, so it enforces nothing. There is no allowlist or identifier validation on `t`. There is no auth middleware on the route. By contrast, vacuum (api.go:33-36) checks the error and aborts.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose error is discarded. There is no allowlist, parameterization or middleware. userFrom (api.go:22) panics if no user is in the context, which only stops requests that have no user set.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so a non-dba user who has a user in the request context reaches the unsanitized `"DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")` at api.go:27. The sibling vacuum checks the error at api.go:33-36. In this file nothing sets the context user, so userFrom (api.go:22) would panic on every request. The finding therefore assumes an upstream middleware sets the user, and the attacker is a low-privilege authenticated user, not an anonymous one.
